I am a consultant, so switching clients happens very often.

One of the things the new clients does, is to make me fill in this excel spread sheet with the experiences I have. And here is the issue, I can never fill in realistic numbers.

I give an example.

I started with C++ back with Turbo C++ 1.0 (1990). I developed in VC 6.0, VC 2001 VC 2002,.... But I never continuous developed in C++. Other jobs, other languages.

So:

  • I have known C++ for 25 years now.
  • I have developed In C++ for about 7 years combined.
  • But the C++ 1.0 is outdated and I have not touched C++ for years now.
  • If you give me a C++ job, within a month I am at full speed again. Need to refresh my memory and adapt to the new C++.

So how would one measure experience?

C++ is just one example, I could have used SQL, Delphi, ASP.NET, .....

I'd call that "7 years experience". If you're going to take a C++ job, just let them know there will be a short ramp-up period. If they're a good employer, they'll be fine with that. If they'll be a shitty employer, they'll not offer you the job and you didn't want it in the first place because they would make your life hell.

Unless the language/framework is really new, I don't even put how many years experience I have with something. I just tell you all of the things I have experience with. I'm not applying unless I think I'm a fit. If you have a problem with my technical expertise it should come out during the interview. If it doesn't, don't blame me for your horrible interviewing standards. Like OP said, I may be rusty with a few things on there but I'll ramp up again quickly.

Measuring competency is hard. It's the same sort of thing as asking a mechanic, "How much experience do you have with wrenches?" or, "How much experience do you have with jack stands?" It's wholly possible to work with C++ exclusively for ten years and still be bad at it. Furthermore, a good mechanic can get dropped into an unfamiliar shop, and within a day or two they'll be humming away nicely, where a shit mechanic would never quite get his footing no matter how much he's got going for him.

My personal recommendation, in this case, is to try to quantify your experience in achievements instead of in 'years' or 'volume' of experience. Providing specific examples of stuff you've done in C++, explaining the domain of the problem you solved--those things tend to be the things that really raise eyebrows.

For myself, for example, I would discuss my most recent work by saying that I 'began educating myself in functional programming as soon as Swift was announced by Apple, and began applying my knowledge to the app on which I work immediately. When Swift 2.0 was announced the following year, I applied its new features to the software I had been writing, and we began integrating my code as the basis of the application the day after Xcode 7.0 Final was released".

That explains how I recognized the applicability of a new tool to an old task, how I went about validating my knowledge while still doing my day job, and how ultimately my solution was recognized as useful by my colleagues and superiors and went into production. Soon, once we've released the code, I'm going to chase down some numbers about how my code's improved our stability.

In your case, as a consultant, I would go back and ask your clients. Ask them, "could you tell me a little bit about how the work I did on _______ project helped you out?" You'll find, if you've done a good job and worked with nice people, that they'll happily tell you about how you did great work that really helped their business. Then, somebody reading your code isn't thinking in terms of, "This guy gets up and running in new languages pretty quick, I bet he could handle this". They're thinking in terms of, "This guy boosted the profits of every company he worked with, and now he's going to boost mine."

It's a two-way street. The recruiter should make sure they get the information they need from the applicant. For example in interviews, in the C++ case, we ask about the systems, the size of the code base, how many in the team, the individuals role in the team, then we focus on language specifics like design patterns. Together with all the other questions we should get a good idea as to the competence of people. In short, the CV should be the entry point to the interview and the experience should be explained in context.

Performant Enum Generic Helpers/Extensions for C#/VB/*.Net (written in C++/CLI and MSIL due to lack of C# enum constraint). Feedback Appreciated.

Can you clarify what you are trying to do and why someone would use your library?

What I mean is, what is the problem your library is trying to solve? I mean in layman's terms it is too abstract what you write.

Well, I'll stick with "what it solved for me", since I wrote it for entirely selfish reasons. The first big one was a pressing problem I had with an application that used the string values of several enums for several processes (it was an app that accessed thousands of machines to perform millions of operations for access auditing purposes). The overhead of the ToString() and HasFlag call was 20% of processing in that case, so I optimised it (HasFlag was simply removed in favor of (flag&flagCheck == flagCheck). I took that implementation and redid it in this library and included a faster implementation of HasFlag (IsFlagSet)

The second motivation came from a discussion I had over an API design choice for an API I didn't write/couldn't modify. They used a non-flags enum to indicate an action and a boolean to indicate its availability in an event handler along with a boolean returning method something along the lines of "CanExecute(NonFlagsEnum.MethodName)" Particularly with this API, a flags enum would have been an obvious and perfect choice. In this discussion, several seasoned developers agreed that "Flags enums are annoying to work with." I kind of had to agree, though I use them all the time. So my aim was to make working with flags enums dead simple and extremely readable.

On the annoying to work with front, you have all of the static enum methods, which require casting, and passing type parameters: An example of ugly: (MyEnum)Enum.Parse(typeof(MyEnum), "MyFirstFlag"); Better: Enums.Parse<MyEnum>("MyFirstFlag"); // returns a MyEnum

GetValues and many others have these same patterns circa .Net pre-generics.

Then there's the conditional statements involving flags. One is fine and easy to parse, but many of my applications had the need to check several flags in various ways. Checking if one flag among a set of flags is set: if ((MyEnumValue & MyEnum.Flag1) == MyEnum.Flag1) || (MyEnumValue & MyEnum.Flag2) == MyEnum.Flag2) || (MyEnumValue & MyEnum.Flag3) == MyEnum.Flag3)) // (did I match all of those damn parens up?) vs if (MyEnumValue.AreAnyFlagsSet(MyEnum.Flag1, MyEnum.Flag2, MyEnum.Flag3)

(There's an AreAllFlagsSet for the similar case with "&"s)

There's an argument to be made that C# developers just don't like operators to check flags -- Microsoft themselves added a (shoddy) HasFlag method for this purpose. It's needlessly slow, but the trade-off is fine in 99% of cases.

Defining an enum is simple enough, and very readable if you use the shifts, but many either aren't aware of that or don't like it for whatever reason (I see hex/decimal notation used most of the time), so I included constants that define each flag F1, F2, F3, and so on (encoded in a type that works with all underlying types).

I had several APIs that preferred a non-flags enum with a boolean to identify the availability of certain actions, either through an event handler that passed in the enum with an "IsAvailable" boolean or a method that took the enum and returned a boolean. In this particular API, using a flags enum would have been perfect, but it was avoided for whatever reason (hopefully not "developers don't like them" since that's a very debatable statement). Their choice added so much code to my application that I implemented "ModifyFlag", "AddFlagIf" and "RemoveFlagIf". ModifyFlag sets on true, unsets on false and is used to convert this odd pattern in one LOC to a flags enum I manage internally: Actions.ModifyFlag(ActionFlags.ActionName, e.IsAvailable) in a switch handles everything for me. My example is a corner case, for sure, but the purpose of flags enums is to give you a way to store ... on/off flags ... so it's really convenient to be able to do that in a line of code that is obvious to anyone reading it (and it discourages the use of a bunch of "related boolean variables" in a class, and encoding as flags can help avoid having to rewrite stored data when features need to be added, so win-win).

The most minor reason, though, was to find something to work on in C++/CLI to further my goal of getting back into C++ development. This turned out to be neutral to bad for that. Because it uses generics, and C++/CLI cannot mix generics and templates (even when mixing them wouldn't result in breakage due to the "generics are unknown at compile-time" rule), it resulted in a lot of messy #defines and repeated method definitions for each underlying type. C++/CLI is also a huge detour from modern C++11/14/1?, but shares a little of the philosophy (not nearly enough). The neutral part was by requirement: C#/VB and AFAIK no other .Net language allows setting a constraint for Enum (all can consume it, none can define it...directly), so C++/CLI was the "only" choice.
